function.name: generate_sea_foam
function.description: Simulates the creation of sea foam based on the agitation level of water, amount of organic material, and the presence of salt. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

agitation_level.description: The level of agitation in the water, represented by a scale from 1 (calm) to 10 (very agitated).

organic_material.description: The amount of organic material present in grams per liter. This is a float type value.

salt_presence.description: Indicates whether salt is present (true) or not (false) in the water.

temperature.description: The water temperature in degrees Celsius. If unspecified, defaults to average sea temperature. This is a float type value.

message.content:
The sea typically looks **blue**—the same hue we see in clear skies. That’s because water absorbs longer wavelengths (red, orange, yellow) more strongly than shorter wavelengths (blue). When sunlight hits the ocean, the blue light is scattered in all directions, giving the water its characteristic tint.

But the color isn’t fixed. It changes with:

| Factor | Effect on Color |
|--------|-----------------|
| **Depth** | Shallow water reflects the color of the bottom (sand, algae, coral), often greenish‑yellow or turquoise. Deeper water absorbs more red light, so it looks darker blue or even indigo. |
| **Angle of Sunlight** | At sunrise/sunset the sun is low; the water can appear reddish or orange because the light passes through more atmosphere and scatters less blue. |
| **Water Clarity** | Turbid or muddy water scatters light differently, often turning the surface brownish or greenish. |
| **Organic Material & Algae** | High concentrations of phytoplankton give a greenish tint; dissolved organic matter can make the water look brown or tea‑colored. |
| **Salt Presence** | Pure freshwater can appear slightly greener; seawater’s salt content doesn’t change the basic scattering mechanism, but the dissolved salts influence the overall clarity and can affect how light is absorbed. |

So while “blue” is the most common descriptor, the sea’s appearance is a dynamic blend of physics, chemistry, and biology.
